subject: playwright
title: Locator strategy
description: Why getByRole beats a CSS chain, what strict mode is actually protecting you from, and how to scope instead of index.

content.title: Locators are lazy
content.body: A locator is not an element — it is a description of how to find one, re-resolved on every action. That is why a locator created before a re-render still works, and why there is no such thing as a stale element reference in Playwright.

content.title: The order to reach for
content.body: Role first, then label or text, then test id. A CSS chain is the last resort: it encodes the DOM shape, which is the part most likely to change.

content.title: Strict mode
content.body: Any action on a locator that matches more than one element throws instead of silently picking the first. That error is a real ambiguity in the page, not Playwright being difficult — .first() hides it, scoping fixes it.

exercises.question: Why is getByRole usually preferred over a CSS selector?

answers.text: It is faster to evaluate in the browser
It targets what the user and assistive tech perceive, so it survives refactors of the markup
It is the only locator that supports auto-waiting
CSS selectors do not work in Playwright

exercises.explanation: Role and accessible name are part of the contract with the user; class names and DOM depth are implementation details. A role locator also fails loudly when accessibility regresses.

exercises.question: The page has three "Delete" buttons, one per row. Which line throws?

answers.text: Line 2 — toHaveCount needs a single element
Line 4 — getByText matches partial strings
Line 3 — the locator resolves to three elements and strict mode refuses to guess
Line 1 — getByRole('row') is not a valid role

exercises.explanation: Assertions on a collection are fine; actions are not. Scope it: page.getByRole('row', { name: 'Invoice 12' }).getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' }).

exercises.question: Which version survives a new row being added at the top of the table?

answers.text: B — it identifies the row by its content, so position does not matter
A — nth() is re-evaluated on every action
Both, because Playwright re-resolves locators
Neither — you have to use a test id

exercises.explanation: Re-resolving does not help when the index itself is the wrong idea. nth() is fine for genuinely positional things ("the first item"), not for identifying a record.

exercises.question: A locator stored in a variable before the page re-renders becomes stale and must be recreated.
exercises.explanation: The locator holds the query, not the element. It is resolved again at the moment of each action or assertion, which is precisely why Playwright has no stale-element errors.

exercises.question: getByText('Save') also matches "Save and close". Complete the call so it matches only the exact label.

answers.text: strict
exact
full
whole

exercises.explanation: Text matching is substring and case-insensitive by default. exact: true makes it case-sensitive and whole-string — and getByRole with a name is usually better still.

exercises.question: You need the list item that contains the text "Overdue" and has a visible "Pay" button. Which reads best?

answers.text: page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'Overdue' }).filter({ has: page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }) })
page.locator('li:has-text("Overdue"):has(button)')
page.getByRole('listitem').nth(0)
page.getByText('Overdue').locator('..')

exercises.explanation: filter() composes readable conditions and keeps the strict-mode guarantee. Climbing with '..' works but couples the test to the DOM shape.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: A data-testid is the right choice when the element has ___ that identifies it for a user.

answers.text: no accessible role or name
more than one role
a dynamic class name
no id attribute

exercises.explanation: Test ids are an escape hatch for genuinely unlabelled elements — a chart canvas, a decorative wrapper. Reaching for them first means accessibility problems never surface in the tests.

exercises.question: The widget renders inside an iframe. What does this do?

answers.text: Times out — page locators do not pierce an iframe, you need frameLocator()
Works — Playwright searches every frame by default
Throws a strict mode violation
Works only if the iframe is same-origin

exercises.explanation: page.frameLocator('#checkout').getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }) crosses the boundary. Shadow DOM is different — locators pierce open shadow roots automatically.

exercises.question: Playwright · locators
exercises.back: Matches the accessible name — substring, case-insensitive, whitespace-normalised
exercises.explanation: Add exact: true when "Save" must not match "Save draft". The accessible name comes from the text, aria-label, or the associated label element.

exercises.question: A colleague fixes a strict mode error by appending .first(). When is that actually correct?

answers.text: Whenever the error appears — it is the documented fix
Only when the page legitimately renders a list and any element of it would do
Never — .first() is deprecated
Only in tests marked as flaky

exercises.explanation: Strict mode caught a real ambiguity. If there should have been one match, .first() converts a clear failure into a test that passes against the wrong element.

exercises.question: Chaining locators (parent.getByRole(...)) narrows the search to that parent's subtree.
exercises.explanation: That is the main tool against strict mode violations: scope to the card, row or dialog you mean, then look for the control inside it.

exercises.question: This selector broke after a CSS-only refactor. Which part is responsible?

answers.text: The .btn-primary class — classes never change
nth-child and the direct-child combinator, which encode the DOM structure
locator() itself — it should be getByTestId
Nothing — CSS refactors cannot affect selectors

exercises.explanation: Anything positional or structural breaks when a wrapper div is added. Role plus accessible name describes the thing the user sees, which is what the refactor kept.
